questions.stem: What is Semantic Segmentation in Computer Vision, and how is it different from image classification and object detection?
options: Semantic segmentation gives a label to the whole image and then describes where attention was focused. Image classification labels individual pixels, while object detection assigns a separate class to every pixel instead of predicting boxes.

Semantic segmentation assigns a category to every image pixel, producing a spatial class map. Image classification gives an overall image label, while object detection predicts object locations, usually as class-labeled bounding boxes with confidence scores.

Semantic segmentation identifies visible objects with rectangular boxes and confidence scores, then merges their boxes into a single scene label. Image classification counts these boxes, while object detection colors all background pixels according to class.

Semantic segmentation identifies each separate object and gives it a unique instance ID, even when objects share a category. Image classification provides only object counts, while object detection labels the complete image without object locations.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Semantic segmentation means assigning a class, such as road, car, or sky, to every pixel. This gives a detailed map of which parts of an image belong to each category. Image classification instead predicts a label for the image as a whole. Object detection finds individual objects and usually draws boxes around them. Picture a street photo: segmentation colors the road, cars, buildings, and people by category, down to their pixels. It does not automatically number individual cars.

01 · VISUAL LESSON

A whole-image label, object boxes, or a full pixel map

Detection localizes instances with boxes; semantic segmentation marks pixel classes. It does not automatically assign a different instance ID to each object.

questions.stem: How does a Semantic Segmentation mask represent per-pixel class labels, background regions, and ignored pixels in a digital image?
options: A segmentation mask stores a class ID for each detected object and repeats that ID across its bounding box, including surrounding background. Unlabeled pixels automatically inherit the closest object's class, so a separate ignore value is unnecessary.

A segmentation mask records one probability score for the entire image and uses that score to color each pixel equally. Background is represented by missing image channels, and ignored pixels are converted to whichever class occurs most often.

A segmentation mask is usually a list of object boxes and their confidences; pixels inside each box are grouped together regardless of category. Background pixels become class zero only when the model predicts no objects anywhere in the image.

A segmentation mask typically stores an integer class ID at each pixel, forming a height-by-width array. Background may have its own class ID, while pixels without reliable labels can use a separate ignore value during training or evaluation.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A semantic mask is a grid that matches an image's height and width. Each position holds a number representing a class. In a satellite image, 0 might mean sky, 1 road, 2 building, and 3 vegetation. The visible colors are just a palette for those numbers. Background can have a real class ID; pixels with uncertain labels may instead use an ignore value so the loss and evaluation skip them. Never confuse class IDs with RGB colors.
questions.figure:
02 · VISUAL LESSON

From a pixel-ID array to a colored land-cover mask

A semantic mask stores class IDs at each pixel (for example 0=sky, 1=road, 2=building, 3=vegetation). Background may be a class; ignored pixels need an explicit ignore value.

questions.stem: Why can Semantic Segmentation identify a class across many pixels but not automatically distinguish separate objects of the same class?
options: Semantic segmentation predicts a category for each pixel, not a separate identity for each object. Two apples therefore share the class apple; instance segmentation adds distinct object masks or IDs when those individual apples must be separated.

Semantic segmentation predicts a category for every pixel and automatically assigns new identity numbers to disconnected regions. Two apples get different instance IDs by default, while instance segmentation combines them into one shared object class.

Semantic segmentation gives each pixel a class but treats nearby pixels of that class as a single object regardless of boundaries. Instance segmentation instead stores one full-image category label and cannot separate the apples as individual objects.

Semantic segmentation labels each visible object's center and extends that label to surrounding pixels without examining edges. It naturally distinguishes every individual apple, while instance segmentation is only useful for objects with different categories.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A semantic mask answers “Which class is this pixel?” rather than “Which individual object owns this pixel?” If a grocery image contains two apples, both receive the class apple. That is useful for estimating how much of the image contains fruit, but not enough to count apples reliably. Instance segmentation separates apple one from apple two with different masks or IDs. Panoptic segmentation combines pixel categories with separate identities for countable objects.
questions.figure:
03 · VISUAL LESSON

Two apples can have one semantic class but separate instance IDs

Semantic segmentation gives the same class to similar objects. Instance segmentation also separates individual objects; panoptic segmentation combines semantic regions and instance identities.

questions.stem: How do encoder-decoder segmentation models such as U-Net use downsampling, upsampling, and skip connections to produce detailed pixel predictions?
options: U-Net downsamples images to learn broad patterns, but its decoder predicts a single global category before returning to full resolution. Skip connections copy the final class label across pixels rather than bringing back spatial feature information.

U-Net downsamples images for context and then upsamples feature maps, but it removes all early spatial information intentionally. Skip connections carry only final image labels into the decoder, making boundary location independent of encoder detail.

U-Net uses an encoder to extract features at smaller resolutions and a decoder to upsample them into a pixel-level prediction. Skip connections combine earlier, higher-resolution features with decoder features, helping restore fine spatial details and boundaries.

U-Net keeps all feature maps at the original image resolution and uses downsampling only after prediction. Skip connections pass decoder outputs backward to replace encoder inputs, so the model learns pixel categories without multi-scale features.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The encoder side of U-Net gradually reduces image resolution while learning broader context, such as what a structure looks like. The decoder increases resolution again to assign a class to each pixel. Skip connections bring useful high-resolution features from the encoder into matching decoder stages. Imagine outlining cells in a microscope image: the deep features help identify a cell, while the earlier details help recover its edges. Upsampling alone can blur boundaries without that finer information.
questions.figure:
04 · VISUAL LESSON

U-Net: down for context, up for pixel detail

Downsampling helps recognize broad patterns; upsampling restores spatial resolution. Skip connections pass earlier fine features to the decoder for sharper boundaries.

questions.stem: How can PyTorch convert per-pixel class scores into a Semantic Segmentation mask, and how should image preprocessing and mask resizing be handled?
options: PyTorch can convert class-score maps into a mask by choosing the highest score along the image height axis. Preprocessing may use any channel order, while training masks should be resized with bilinear interpolation to preserve smooth class IDs.

PyTorch can produce per-pixel class logits shaped [batch, classes, height, width] and select the highest-scoring class along the class axis. Use consistent input preprocessing; resize logits appropriately and use nearest-neighbor interpolation for discrete masks.

PyTorch converts per-pixel logits into a mask by averaging scores across all classes at each location. Resize the resulting integer labels with bilinear interpolation, because fractional values improve boundary accuracy when converted back to class numbers.

PyTorch can produce class logits for every pixel, but should choose the largest score over the entire image at once. Preprocessing and resizing can change pixel alignment freely because segmentation output concerns categories rather than exact positions.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A segmentation model usually returns one score per class at each pixel. In PyTorch, logits often have shape [batch, classes, height, width]. Taking argmax along the class dimension gives the predicted class ID at each location. The code below uses a tiny untrained model only to demonstrate the shapes—not real segmentation accuracy. For a trained model, preprocess images exactly as expected, resize class-score maps before argmax when needed, and use nearest-neighbor interpolation for integer target masks.
questions.figure:
05 · VISUAL LESSON

Pixel logits → argmax → segmentation mask

Python · PyTorch mask creation 12 lines · runnable shape example
import torch
from torch import nn
torch.manual_seed(5)
image = torch.rand(1, 3, 64, 64)    # sample RGB
model = nn.Conv2d(3, 3, 1).eval()   # toy model
with torch.no_grad():
    logits = model(image)           # [1, 3, H, W]
    mask = logits.argmax(dim=1)[0] # [H, W]
palette = torch.tensor([[92,166,209],
    [68,170,133], [230,159,83]], dtype=torch.uint8)
rgb_mask = palette[mask]
print(mask.shape, rgb_mask.shape)

Expected output: torch.Size([64, 64]) and torch.Size([64, 64, 3]). This tiny model is untrained: its mask is illustrative, not a meaningful prediction.

Use consistent RGB preprocessing and resize logits to the target resolution before argmax if needed. For resizing discrete annotation masks, use nearest-neighbor interpolation.

questions.tag: Advanced · IoU, Dice and class balance
questions.stem: How are Intersection over Union (IoU), Dice score, and mean IoU used to evaluate Semantic Segmentation, and why must class imbalance be considered?
options: IoU divides shared foreground pixels by the number of ground-truth pixels, and Dice divides shared pixels by the predicted pixels. Mean IoU then gives larger classes more influence, which makes rare classes less important during model evaluation.

IoU compares a prediction to ground truth using overlap divided by total predicted pixels, while Dice compares only class labels without spatial overlap. Mean IoU measures the overall percentage of correctly predicted pixels, including background frequency.

IoU and Dice both score foreground overlap, but IoU uses the sum of predicted and true areas without subtracting shared pixels. Mean IoU is calculated from confidence scores rather than class masks, so class imbalance does not affect interpretation.

IoU divides the shared pixel area by the union of predicted and true areas. Dice uses twice the overlap divided by their total areas. Mean IoU averages class scores; rare classes still need separate inspection when background dominates.
questions.explanation: Explanation: IoU asks how much the predicted region overlaps the true region relative to their union. Dice also measures overlap but divides twice the shared area by the sum of predicted and true areas. For a class with 8 shared pixels, 10 true pixels, and 12 predicted pixels, IoU is 8/14 ≈ 0.571 and Dice is 16/22 ≈ 0.727. Mean IoU averages class IoUs, usually giving classes equal weight. Always inspect rare classes and boundaries, not just overall pixel accuracy.
questions.figure:
06 · VISUAL LESSON

Count overlap, missed pixels and extra pixels

IoU divides shared pixels by all predicted-or-true foreground pixels. Dice rewards overlap using twice the intersection. Check minority classes separately instead of relying on dominant background accuracy.

questions.stem: How should Semantic Segmentation systems handle domain shift, annotation quality, class imbalance, data leakage, and inference constraints in real-world deployment?
options: Deployment should select preprocessing and thresholds using the final test set, then track average pixel accuracy on new images. A large training set compensates for label mistakes, so rare-class quality and device latency only need checking at launch.

Deployment should prioritize fast pixel labeling on representative training images and reuse the same sites in final tests to improve consistency. Domain shift can be handled by recoloring results, while noisy labels are corrected through higher confidence thresholds.

Deployment should audit masks and boundaries, use leakage-resistant splits, measure per-class performance across changed environments, and test latency and memory on actual hardware. Monitor rare-class failures, input drift, and annotation quality after release.

Deployment should maximize image resolution and model size to improve boundaries, since accurate segmentation automatically stays reliable under new lighting or seasons. Validation and leakage checks can be skipped when pixel-level training loss becomes sufficiently small.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A model that segments a clear field image may struggle with shadows, new seasons, or a different camera. Before release, verify annotation boundaries and rare classes, and split data by site or time when images are related. This reduces leakage from nearly identical scenes. Evaluate per-class IoU, small-region mistakes, and latency on the real device. After release, monitor lighting changes, missed regions, performance drift, and new data quality. Do not assume high training accuracy proves reliable field performance.

07 · VISUAL LESSON

A good mask must survive real-world changes

p95 latencyReal deployment hardware
Data integrity: keep sites, people or time periods from leaking between train and test splits.
Monitoring: test seasonal shifts, rare classes, calibration, failures and changes in input quality.

Deployment checks should include annotation quality, patient/site/time-aware splits when relevant, distribution shifts, minority-class errors, device speed, privacy safeguards and retraining triggers.
